questions.q: How do I measure the ROI of an AI tool?
questions.a: Check whether it saves you money, makes you money or helps your team do more with less. Set targets for those outcomes before you roll it out, such as revenue from conversion or retention, lower labor or training costs, or more output per employee. Clear targets make it easy to judge results and drop what doesn't deliver.

questions.q: What are signs that an AI tool isn't worth the cost?
questions.a: Warning signs include a tool nobody uses, or one people use while still making decisions the same way as before. If you can't say whether you're faster, whether margins improved or whether any revenue lift came from it, the tool likely fails the test. Impressive demos and sleek dashboards don't count as returns on their own.

questions.q: Why is a 'good enough' AI tool risky to keep?
questions.a: A tool that works well enough to keep but never scales quietly drains your budget like legacy software. Teams often hold on because of the months they spent integrating it. Meanwhile, simpler and more outcome-focused options get stuck waiting for approval.

questions.q: What kind of AI delivers the most value for a business?
questions.a: Often it's AI that runs behind your workflows, routing customer issues, syncing menus or surfacing loyalty insights from guest feedback. When your team relies on it every day, it becomes a force multiplier. That's where returns tend to show up consistently across the business.
